name: New Mexico

notes: Food sold by grocery stores is deductible from the state and local gross receipts tax (NMSA 7-9-92); prepared food is taxed in full.

Alcohol pays the gross receipts tax plus the wholesalers' liquor excise tax, left out here: spirits $1.60 a liter, beer 41 cents a gallon (small brewers 8 cents), wine 45 cents a liter, cider 41 cents a gallon.

Cigarettes and other tobacco pay the gross receipts tax plus excise taxes left out here: $2.00 a pack of cigarettes, 25% of the price on other tobacco and nicotine pouches, and 12.5% on e-cigarettes (50 cents a cartridge of 5 ml or less).
Household supplies: diapers are taxed in full; a 2023 bill to make them deductible (HB 222) died in committee, and no deduction is on TRD pages.
Personal care products: menstrual products have been deductible since July 1, 2022 (NMSA 7-9-120), which is not taken out here.
Barber and beauty services, laundry and dry cleaning, and auto repair labor: gross receipts tax applies to services.
Clothing is taxed, except clothing and shoes under $100 during the back-to-school holiday, July 31 to August 2, 2026, at retailers that took part.
Motor fuel is exempt from the gross receipts tax and pays a 17-cent-a-gallon gasoline tax plus a petroleum loading fee instead, left out here.
The gross receipts tax is levied on sellers and usually passed on; the total rate combines state, county and municipal rates.
Restaurant meals pay the full combined rate; New Mexico's cities and counties levy no separate restaurant tax.
The Small Business Saturday deduction for small retailers ended July 1, 2025; a 2025 bill to extend it to 2030 (HB 179) was not confirmed enacted, and it is not counted here.

Hotel stays pay the combined rate plus a local lodgers' tax of up to 5% and, in Albuquerque, a 1% hospitality fee on room rent (City of Albuquerque) and, in Santa Fe, a 2% convention center fee (City of Santa Fe Ordinance 2021-11); not counted here.
gaps: 49 tax increment district rows and 11 airport, park, fairground and facility rows on the schedule are not used; tax increment districts charge the rate of the city or county around them.

Tribal lands aren't used here, and several pueblo rates on the schedule (sales by non-members to non-members) differ from the county rate around them: Acoma 8%, Kewa 7.5%, Santa Ana 7.2%, Pojoaque and Tesuque 7.125%, San Ildefonso 7%, Sandia 6.4375% and Jemez 6.25%; at Isleta, sales to the tribe and its members are untaxed (0%). The Navajo Nation charges its own 6% sales tax on retail sales there and a 2% tax on junk food (as reported), and the Mescalero Apache and Ute Mountain lands aren't on the schedule; none of these is counted.

Taos County's El Prado and El Valle de Los Ranchos water and sanitation districts add 0.25% inside them (7.75% outside the town of Taos, 9.425% where a district overlaps the town); not counted, since their boundaries don't follow Census places (noted on the pages of Taos, Ranchos de Taos and Taos County).
GRT applies to most services as well as goods, so it is broader than a typical sales tax.

programs: Tax increment districts aren't mapped except Albuquerque's two downtown redevelopment areas (Downtown and West Central): the Taxation and Revenue Department's rate layer lists about 50 others (among them Las Cruces' Downtown district and its redevelopment areas, Albuquerque's Mesa del Sol, Winrock and Lower Petroglyphs districts, Bernalillo County's Santolina and Upper Petroglyphs districts, Rio Rancho's Los Diamantes, Stonegate and Village at Rio Rancho, and the Taos Ski Valley district), which charge the surrounding rate. The state's 11 Arts and Cultural Districts (Downtown Albuquerque, Artesia, Carlsbad, Farmington, Gallup, Las Cruces, Las Vegas, Los Alamos, Mora, Raton and Silver City) and its MainStreet communities have no map layer.
